_about: Notes on the physical and social world of a passage: places, buildings, coins, customs, rulers and archaeology. Written for this app in its own words. Each note carries a label for how firm it is: 'attested' (an inscription or an artefact names or shows it), 'documented' (ancient writers describe it), 'supported' (archaeology fits the picture), 'proposed' (a reconstruction), 'traditional' (an old identification, not proved) or 'disputed'.

entries.title: The Temple treasury and the widow's two coins
entries.note: The offering chests stood in the Court of the Women; the Mishnah (Shekalim 6:5) describes thirteen trumpet-shaped receptacles. The widow gave two lepta, the smallest bronze coin in circulation. Mark explains that two lepta make one quadrans (a Roman coin). Lepta from this period are common finds, so the scene needs no reconstruction of the money, only of the exact spot in the Temple court.

entries.title: A house at Capernaum and a roof opened
entries.note: Village houses were built of local basalt stone with flat roofs of wooden beams, branches and packed clay, reached by outside stairs; opening such a roof is physically plausible. Excavations at Capernaum found a first-century house complex under a later church, which Christians venerated early as Peter's house; the identification is traditional, supported by the early veneration but not proved.

entries.title: Capernaum and its Roman presence
entries.note: Capernaum lay on the road and the border between the territories of Herod Antipas and Philip, so a customs post and a small garrison fit the setting (Mark 2:14). The visible white limestone synagogue at the site dates from late antiquity; some scholars think it stands over an earlier basalt building of the first century.

entries.title: The denarius with Caesar's image
entries.note: The silver denarius of Tiberius bore the emperor's head and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus. Such coins are found in great numbers. A denarius was roughly a labourer's daily wage (Matthew 20:2).

entries.title: The Temple tax and the coin in the fish's mouth
entries.note: Every adult Jewish male paid a half-shekel Temple tax each year (Exodus 30:11-16; Mishnah Shekalim). It had to be paid in Tyrian silver, which was valued for its purity. A stater, the coin in the story, was the equivalent of a shekel: enough for two people.

entries.title: The six stone water jars at Cana
entries.note: Stone vessels were popular in Jewish households of this period because stone was believed not to contract ritual impurity (Mishnah Kelim 10). Workshops that turned and carved such vessels have been found near Jerusalem and in Galilee, and large stone jars of this kind are known.

entries.title: The pool of Bethesda
entries.note: Excavations near the Church of St Anne in Jerusalem uncovered a double pool with colonnades on four sides and one in the middle, matching John's 'five porticoes'. The site was later used as a healing sanctuary.

entries.title: The pool of Siloam
entries.note: In 2004 a stepped pool of the Second Temple period was exposed at the southern end of the City of David and identified as the Siloam of John 9. Hezekiah's water tunnel, which feeds it, carries an inscription (the Siloam inscription) describing its completion.

entries.title: Jacob's well
entries.note: A very deep well lies at the foot of Mount Gerizim near ancient Shechem and has been venerated since at least the fourth century as Jacob's well. John's note that the well was deep fits the site.

entries.title: The rulers named by Luke
entries.note: Luke dates the call of John the Baptist by six rulers. Tiberius, Pontius Pilate and Herod Antipas are well known. An inscription from Abila names a Lysanias as tetrarch in the reign of Tiberius, which supports Luke's mention of 'Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene'.

entries.title: Pontius Pilate
entries.note: A limestone block found at Caesarea Maritima in 1961 carries an inscription naming Pontius Pilate as prefect of Judea. It is the only inscription that names him, and it confirms his title.

entries.title: Caiaphas the high priest
entries.note: An ornate ossuary found in a Jerusalem tomb in 1990 carries the name 'Joseph son of Caiaphas'. Many scholars identify the occupant with the high priest of the Gospels, who ruled about AD 18–36; others are cautious.

entries.title: The census under Quirinius
entries.note: Josephus (Antiquities 18.1) records a census of Judea under Quirinius in AD 6, and Luke places the birth of Jesus in the reign of Herod, who died in 4 BC. Scholars have proposed several ways of reading the evidence: an earlier enrolment, a different sense of Luke's wording, or a loose dating. None is universally accepted.

entries.title: Herod the Great and his buildings
entries.note: Herod built Herodium near Bethlehem as a fortress-palace, and his tomb was identified there in 2007. His cruelty in his last years is described by Josephus, which fits the Gospel picture of a ruler who feared a rival king.

entries.title: The Magi
entries.note: Matthew does not say how many Magi came, or give their names; the number three comes from the three gifts. 'Magi' were Persian or Babylonian priests and astrologers. Attempts to date the star by comets or planetary conjunctions are possible suggestions, not established facts.

entries.title: The Temple's great stones thrown down
entries.note: Excavations along the foot of the Western Wall found the pavement of a Herodian street covered by great ashlar blocks that fell from the Temple Mount's walls when the Romans destroyed it in AD 70. The finds match Jesus's words about the stones being thrown down.

entries.title: Whitewashed tombs
entries.note: The Mishnah (Shekalim 1:1) says graves were whitewashed each spring before Passover so that pilgrims would not touch them by accident and become ritually impure. It explains why a whitewashed tomb looks clean from the outside.

entries.title: Tombs in the hillsides
entries.note: Many first-century rock-cut tombs have been found in Galilee and Judea, entered by a low opening and closed with a stone.

entries.title: Burial and the tomb of Joseph of Arimathea
entries.note: Wealthy families cut tombs with a rolling stone and a bench for the body; the Herodian family tomb in Jerusalem has a rolling-stone door. The traditional site, under the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, lies inside a quarry that held first-century tombs. The identification goes back to Constantine's builders in the fourth century and is traditional; the tomb itself has been rebuilt many times.

entries.title: Four days in the tomb
entries.note: In Jerusalem in this period bodies were laid in a tomb and the bones collected into an ossuary after about a year, so a tomb could be reopened. The mourning, the wrapping in linen and the stone are consistent with the evidence.

entries.title: Sowing the seed
entries.note: Farmers broadcast seed by hand before ploughing it in, so seed fell on paths, thin soil over limestone, and thorny ground. The pictures in the parable are ordinary farming.

entries.title: The mustard seed
entries.note: The black mustard seed is tiny and the plant can grow to the height of a small tree, up to about three metres, in a season. 'The smallest of all seeds' is a proverbial way of speaking, not a botanical claim.

entries.title: Wineskins
entries.note: Wine was stored in animal skins. New wine still ferments and stretches a new skin; an old skin is stiff and bursts.

entries.title: The millstone
entries.note: The 'millstone' here is the large upper stone turned by a donkey, not the small hand mill. The saying is a very strong image.

entries.title: The prodigal son and the pigs
entries.note: Pigs were unclean for Jews (Leviticus 11:7), so feeding them shows how far the son had fallen. The 'pods' he envied were carob pods used as animal feed.

entries.title: Phylacteries and tassels
entries.note: Phylacteries (small boxes with Scripture texts bound to the arm and forehead) were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran, showing the practice was current in the first century.

entries.title: The road from Jerusalem to Jericho
entries.note: The road drops about 1,000 metres in some 27 kilometres through desert with caves, and it was known as dangerous. The setting suits a story of robbers.

entries.title: The upper room and the Passover meal
entries.note: The Passover lamb was killed in the Temple on the afternoon of 14 Nisan and eaten in Jerusalem that night, by groups gathered in rooms. The Mishnah's Pesachim tractate describes the later form of the meal, including four cups of wine.

entries.title: Foot washing
entries.note: Washing a guest's feet was the task of a servant, or the lowest slave in the house. It makes the gesture of Jesus unmistakably humbling.

entries.title: The soldiers and the seamless tunic
entries.note: Roman custom allowed executioners to keep the clothes of those they crucified.

entries.title: Crucifixion
entries.note: A heel bone with an iron nail still through it was found in a Jerusalem ossuary of a man crucified in the first century, so crucifixion in Judea is directly attested. Roman writers describe the practice.

entries.title: Gallio at Corinth
entries.note: An inscription at Delphi preserves a letter of Claudius naming Gallio proconsul of Achaia; it dates his term to about AD 51–52, one of the firmest anchor points in the chronology of Paul.

entries.title: Athens and the altar to an unknown god
entries.note: Ancient writers (such as Pausanias) mention altars to unnamed or unknown gods at Athens. The Areopagus stood northwest of the Acropolis.

entries.title: The politarchs of Thessalonica
entries.note: Luke calls the city magistrates 'politarchs', a word that did not appear in classical Greek literature, but inscriptions from Thessalonica and other Macedonian cities use it.

entries.title: The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus
entries.note: The great temple was among the Seven Wonders, and its foundations survive. Inscriptions mention a 'temple warden' (neokoros) and a theatre where assemblies met, as in Luke's account.

entries.title: Erastus the city treasurer
entries.note: A paving stone at Corinth carries an inscription recording that an Erastus paid for the pavement as aedile. Some scholars identify him with Paul's Erastus; others think the name was too common to be sure.

entries.title: The death of Herod Agrippa I
entries.note: Josephus (Antiquities 19.8.2) gives an independent account of the king's sudden death at Caesarea in AD 44, in the middle of a festival, in a way that parallels Luke.

entries.title: The street called Straight
entries.note: The main east-west street of Roman Damascus survives as a long street in the old city. Its line is traditionally identified with Luke's 'Straight Street'.

entries.title: Meat sacrificed to idols
entries.note: Much of the meat sold in the market of a Greek city had been offered at a temple first. Corinth had a market building (macellum) and dining rooms attached to temples, which is the world Paul assumes.

entries.title: The games
entries.note: The Isthmian Games, held near Corinth every two years, were among the great athletic festivals. Paul's pictures of training, running and the prize come from them.

entries.title: The praetorian guard and Caesar's household
entries.note: The imperial household included slaves and freedmen throughout Rome and the provinces. Inscriptions mention them, which makes 'those of Caesar's household' unremarkable.

entries.title: Laodicea and lukewarm water
entries.note: The city lay near hot springs at Hierapolis and cold water at Colossae, and its water came by aqueduct from afar, so it is often said the 'lukewarm' image refers to its water. Some scholars think the picture is about useless or half-hearted faith, not temperature.

entries.title: Pergamum and 'Satan's throne'
entries.note: Pergamum was a centre of the cult of the emperor and had a great altar to Zeus. Suggestions for 'Satan's throne' include the altar, the temple of Asclepius and the imperial cult.

entries.title: The number of the beast
entries.note: Some ancient manuscripts read 666 and some 616. Many scholars see a numerical value of the name 'Nero Caesar' in Hebrew letters for 666, and a Latin spelling for 616. Other readings of the number have been suggested.

entries.title: Babel and the ziggurat
entries.note: Mesopotamian cities had temple towers (ziggurats) built of baked brick and bitumen, as in the story. The best-known example at Babylon was called Etemenanki. Whether the story has one particular tower in mind is not known.

entries.title: The cave of Machpelah at Hebron
entries.note: A great Herodian enclosure still stands at Hebron over the traditional site of the burial place of the patriarchs. It is the oldest part of the building and dates from the first century BC; what lies below it is not known.

entries.title: The store cities of Pithom and Ramesses
entries.note: Ramesses is generally identified with Pi-Ramesses, the capital of Ramesses II in the eastern Delta (modern Qantir). The place name Pithom may refer to Tell el-Retaba or Tell el-Maskhuta. Scholars differ about when and how to date these cities to the Exodus tradition.

entries.title: The priestly blessing in silver
entries.note: Two small silver scrolls found in a burial cave at Ketef Hinnom, near Jerusalem, contain a form of the priestly blessing in Hebrew. They date from about the seventh to sixth century BC, and are among the oldest known fragments of biblical text.

entries.title: Jericho
entries.note: Excavators have disagreed about whether walls were standing at Jericho when Israel arrived, and about the dating of destroyed layers. The archaeological picture does not settle the question of the conquest.

entries.title: Goliath and Philistine Gath
entries.note: Excavations at Tell es-Safi (Gath) have uncovered a large Philistine city. A pottery fragment from the tenth or ninth century BC carries two names of non-Semitic, Philistine type, similar to the name Goliath.

entries.title: David's conquest of Jerusalem
entries.note: The Ophel and the City of David show a settled city in David's time, though scholars disagree about how big and wealthy it was in the tenth century BC.

entries.title: Solomon's Temple
entries.note: The Temple Mount cannot be excavated, so no remains of Solomon's temple have been found. Its plan, with porch, main hall and inner shrine, has close parallels in Syrian temples such as those at Ain Dara and Tell Tayinat.

entries.title: Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer
entries.note: Six-chambered gates and large buildings found at all three cities were once attributed to Solomon. Later work has led to a debate about whether they date to his time or to a slightly later period.

entries.title: Jehu on the Black Obelisk
entries.note: An Assyrian monument of about 825 BC, the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III, shows an Israelite king bowing in tribute, labelled 'Jehu, son of Omri'. It is the only contemporary picture of an Israelite king.

entries.title: The Mesha Stele
entries.note: A ninth-century BC Moabite inscription by King Mesha tells of his revolt against Israel, names Omri, and mentions the Lord (YHWH) and Israel's king, in language close to the Bible's account.

entries.title: The Tel Dan stele
entries.note: A fragmentary ninth-century BC Aramaic inscription from Tel Dan speaks of the 'House of David', the earliest known reference to David's dynasty outside the Bible.

entries.title: Sennacherib and Hezekiah
entries.note: Sennacherib's own annals (the Taylor Prism) say he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem 'like a bird in a cage' in 701 BC but do not say he took the city. His reliefs of the siege of Lachish are in the British Museum, and Hezekiah's water tunnel survives.

entries.title: Hezekiah's tunnel
entries.note: A rock-cut tunnel about 533 metres long runs from the Gihon spring to the Pool of Siloam, and an inscription inside it describes the two teams of diggers meeting.

entries.title: Sargon II and Ashdod
entries.note: Isaiah names Sargon, king of Assyria, whom no other biblical book mentions. Sargon's own inscriptions record his capture of Ashdod in 711 BC.

entries.title: Baruch's scribes and seals
entries.note: Clay seal impressions found in Jerusalem name officials who appear in Jeremiah's book, such as 'Gemariah son of Shaphan'. They show that the book's names belong to the period.

entries.title: The fall of Jerusalem in 587/586 BC
entries.note: A burnt layer of destruction in Jerusalem and the Babylonian Chronicle, which records the capture of the city in 597, agree with the Bible's account of the two Babylonian attacks.

entries.title: Judeans in Babylonia
entries.note: Clay tablets from a village called Al-Yahudu ('town of the Judeans') record Judean families living in Babylonia in the sixth to fifth centuries BC.

entries.title: Belshazzar
entries.note: Cuneiform texts name Belshazzar as the crown prince, who ruled in Babylon while his father Nabonidus was in Arabia. The Bible calls him 'king', which fits that role of co-regent. Whether Daniel's account is history or a literary story is debated.

entries.title: The Cyrus Cylinder
entries.note: A clay cylinder from Babylon records Cyrus's policy after taking the city in 539 BC of returning images and peoples to their homelands and rebuilding their temples. It does not name the Jews, but it matches the policy Ezra 1 describes.

entries.title: Sanballat and the Elephantine papyri
entries.note: Jewish soldiers' letters from the island of Elephantine in Egypt (about 407 BC) mention Sanballat, governor of Samaria, and his sons, and ask the governor of Judah for help to rebuild their temple.

entries.title: Ahasuerus and Persian Susa
entries.note: Ahasuerus is the Hebrew form of the Persian name of Xerxes I (486–465 BC). The palace at Susa and the great banquets match what Herodotus and excavations show of the Persian court.

entries.title: The earthquake in Amos's day
entries.note: Excavators at Hazor and other sites have found damage from a large earthquake in the middle of the eighth century BC, which some link with the earthquake mentioned in Amos 1:1 and Zechariah 14:5.

entries.title: Ahaz and Tiglath-Pileser III
entries.note: The annals of the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser III mention Menahem and Pekah of Israel and Ahaz of Judah, the kings of Isaiah 7 and 2 Kings 15–16.

entries.title: Gleaning
entries.note: The law gave the poor the right to gather what the reapers left at the field's edges. The 'ephah' of barley Ruth gleans in a day is about 22 litres of grain.

entries.title: Passover
entries.note: The Passover lamb, the unleavened bread and the bitter herbs are described in Exodus 12–13. The details of the later Passover meal are recorded in Jewish sources from about AD 200 and after, so they cannot be read back into the first Passover without care.

entries.title: The shepherd's rod and staff
entries.note: A shepherd carried a short club or rod to drive off wild animals and a longer staff to guide and rescue sheep. The 'table prepared' and the oil on the head belong to the picture of a host.

entries.title: The tabernacle
entries.note: No remains of the tabernacle have been found. A portable tent shrine is not unknown in the ancient Near East; Egyptian and other ancient texts describe tent sanctuaries, and the plan in Exodus resembles a smaller version of a temple.

entries.title: The Sea of Galilee and its fishing
entries.note: A fishing boat of the first century, preserved in the mud of the lake shore in 1986, is 8.2 metres long and fits the 'boats' of the Gospels. The lake teemed with fish such as tilapia (St Peter's fish).

entries.title: Storms on the Sea of Galilee
entries.note: The lake lies about 210 metres below sea level and is surrounded by hills, so cold winds from the Golan can bring sudden storms. Josephus and local fishermen describe them.

entries.title: Jericho and sycamore trees
entries.note: Jericho in the first century was Herod's winter capital, with palaces and a tax office for the lucrative balsam and date trade, which fits a chief tax collector. The sycamore fig tree is a large tree with low branches.

entries.title: Money changers and sacrificial animals
entries.note: Pilgrims had to pay the Temple tax in Tyrian coin and buy unblemished animals for sacrifice, so money changers and sellers were stationed in the outer court. A series of inscriptions marks the limits that Gentiles could not pass.

entries.title: Mount of the Beatitudes
entries.note: The traditional site is a hill above the north-west shore of the Sea of Galilee, near Capernaum and Tabgha, long venerated by Christians. The Gospels do not name the mountain; Luke has the sermon on a level place.

entries.title: Caesarea Philippi
entries.note: The city lay at the foot of Mount Hermon by a spring and a cave shrine of the god Pan, and Herod Philip rebuilt it. Many see significance in Jesus's naming Peter the rock in front of that rocky cliff, though the Gospel does not say so.

entries.title: The priestly course of Abijah
entries.note: King David divided the priests into twenty-four divisions that served in the Temple in turn for a week twice a year (1 Chronicles 24). Abijah was the eighth (1 Chronicles 24:10).
